你的感觉是对的。让我告诉你原因：

- 你使用的模型 ID 只是一个用于路由的别名

Keeping an open-weight AI model on your laptop is a smart safeguard against subscription price hikes, sudden policy changes, and privacy risks.

Both Ollama and Jan are top-tier, open-source tools for running Large Language Models (LLMs) like Qwen, Gemma, and Llama 3 locally and offline on your machine. However, they are built for two very different types of workflows

Ollama is a lightweight, developer-first background service and CLI, while Jan is a polished, all-in-one desktop GUI application designed as an offline alternative to ChatGPT.

Ollama acts as a local model manager and background server (much like Docker, but for AI models). It is designed to be fast, scriptable, and easily integrated into other applications.

Download the installer from 
http://
ollama.com (available for macOS, Windows, and Linux), or install via package managers (brew install ollama on Mac, or a one-line curl script on Linux).

Pros:
Ultra-lightweight, Unmatched Ecosystem Integration, Fastest Setup
Cons: No Native GUI, Curated Library

Jan (The All-in-One Desktop App)
Jan (
http://
jan.ai) is an open-source, privacy-focused desktop application that gives you a sleek, ChatGPT-like visual interface right out of the box, with a local inference engine (Cortex) built underneath.

Download the desktop installer (.dmg, .exe, or .deb/.AppImage) from 
http://
jan.ai and launch the app.

Pros: Zero Terminal Required, Transparent File System, Ready-to-Use Chat Experience.

Cons: Higher Memory Overhead, Less Suited for Headless/Server Use.

Choose Ollama if you want a clean, fast background service to run models via the terminal, test local endpoints in Postman, wire into Python/Java services, or pair with a Dockerized frontend like Open WebUI.

Choose Jan if you want a single click-and-install desktop icon that gives you a complete, visual, offline ChatGPT workspace with saved chat threads right away.

You can install both and even configure Jan to use Ollama's models as its backend so you don't duplicate model downloads on your hard drive!

An independent musician can own their songs, have a loyal audience, and still struggle to find the money needed to produce the next album.

That's one of the problems 
@IPXExchange
 is trying to address through tokenized intellectual property.

Instead of giving up ownership just to raise funds, creators could use project-based fundraising while keeping control of their original work. The model also includes KPI-gated escrow, where funding is connected to approved production milestones rather than being released all at once.

But there's one detail I think deserves more attention.

Supporting an album through tokens doesn't automatically mean having rights to its future revenue. Ownership, investment, and royalty sharing are three different things.

Clear terms around revenue rights will be important for both creators and investors.

Because funding creative work is one thing, building a fair system where everyone understands what they own is what really matters.

The Floor Is Not

The model sits in a dark field. Five pillars stand in a row, and the one in the middle rises higher than the rest. Out of its top climbs a stack: a glossy slab at the base, a band of something like nerve fibre, a glowing sphere, and at the crown a faint latticed globe, drawn in wire. The pillars on either side are shorter and plainer, and each stands alone, with a clear gap between it and its neighbours. A cluster of pale boxes hangs off the second pillar like notes pinned to a wall. In front of it all is a plaque with a dashed border. It defines a single word, and beneath the definition, in smaller letters, it says: Working hypothesis, not established fact. Along the floor, in a thin line of text the eye almost slides past, runs one sentence. The model is yours. The floor is not.

The word on the plaque is simulation, and the key beside the model explains why it took a building rather than a slogan. A solid shape means settled. A shape with softened, half-transparent walls means contested. A wireframe means speculation. A ghosted shape is history, not a claim at all. Colour means nothing. The model is built to show the one thing that news about simulation almost never carries, which is how sure anyone actually is.

That news has been loud. In April 2025 Franco Vazza, an astrophysicist at the University of Bologna, published a paper in Frontiers in Physics whose title said it is nearly impossible that we live in a simulation. A science site greeted it with the line “it looks like we’re in base reality.” That summer four physicists, Mir Faizal, Lawrence Krauss, Arshid Shabir and Francesco Marino, argued from Gödel’s incompleteness theorems that no purely algorithmic theory of everything can exist, and their abstract drew the conclusion that the universe cannot be a simulation. In November David Wolpert of the Santa Fe Institute published a formal framework in which it is mathematically possible for us to be a simulation running on a computer, and for that computer to be run by us. In March 2026 the physicist Sabine Hossenfelder, who five years earlier had called the simulation hypothesis pseudoscience, told her viewers it was slowly becoming more scientific. Proof against, proof for, a formalism, a sceptic softening. Read quickly, the scoreboard moves every few months.

Read slowly, and nearly all of it concerns one meaning of the word, while the feeling it produces attaches to another.

The model’s five pillars are five meanings, and the gaps between them are the point. The first is the sign. The French theorist Jean Baudrillard, in Simulacra and Simulation in 1981, wrote about copies that have come loose from any original, images that refer to other images until the thing they once stood for has dropped away. The second is the computer: a world produced by a process running on some machine, the meaning the headlines use. The third is the brain. In the framework neuroscientists call predictive processing, the brain doesn’t wait for the world to arrive. It builds a running model of what is out there, sends predictions down to meet the incoming signal, and corrects itself on the errors. The fourth is the offline mind: dreams, daydreams, fiction and myth, which recombine what the model already holds with no live input arriving. The fifth is the engineered model, the digital twin of a jet engine or a power grid, built by people, checked against the real thing, and openly second to it.

The five share a word and a family likeness. They don’t share a mechanism or a body of evidence. Between the third pillar and the second, the model draws a bridge that breaks in the middle, with a label: shared word, not shared mechanism. The break is the most common error in the whole conversation. Talk about living in a computer usually borrows its seriousness from the brain research, which is real, well funded and solid at its core. Then it spends that seriousness on the computer meaning, where nothing comparable has been shown.

The computer meaning usually starts with Nick Bostrom, the Oxford philosopher whose 2003 paper in the Philosophical Quarterly asked, in its title, whether you are living in a computer simulation. The paper is constantly quoted as saying yes. It doesn’t. It argues that at least one of three things is true. Humanity very likely dies out before reaching a technologically mature stage, or mature civilisations almost never bother running detailed simulations of their ancestors, or we are almost certainly living in one. That’s a trilemma, a choice among three, and the paper doesn’t pick. The model hangs it among the pale boxes on the computer pillar with its own correction attached: a trilemma, not a claim.

Bostrom’s paper also contains a sentence that matters later. The simulations it imagines are of people, of minds. If the surrounding environment is simulated too, he wrote, the extra computing power depends on how much of it is rendered and at what grain. The argument is about simulated experience. A whole universe rendered to the last particle is a different and much more expensive proposition.

The argument has been reworked since. Teruji Thomas of Oxford’s Global Priorities Institute published a new version in the journal Erkenntnis in December 2024. It claims we are much more likely to be living in a simulation than on the ground floor of reality, and it’s built to get around objections that had stuck to Bostrom’s version. It carries an odd corollary: discovering that many simulations are being run, or running them ourselves, need not raise the odds that we are in one. This is careful philosophy, and it’s contested. No observation decides it.

The physics, read paper by paper, turns out to be a set of pairs, and in each pair the two sides argue past each other at a particular seam.

Vazza’s paper is real physics. It starts from the principle that information is physical, so storing and processing it costs energy, and it prices three jobs: simulating the visible universe, simulating Earth alone, and simulating a low-resolution Earth just fine enough to fool the neutrino detectors that catch the highest-energy particles. Every version comes out impossible or astronomically costly for a simulator living under physics like ours. The abstract is careful about what follows: only a universe with very different physical properties could run this one. In 2026 the same journal published a commentary on the paper by Eliott Edge and Chad Ashton Brown. Set Vazza beside Bostrom’s own sentence and the seam is plain. Vazza priced a universe. The argument he answered asked about minds. A refutation of the expensive version leaves the cheap version standing, and the cheap version is the one the philosophers were discussing.

The second pair is about logic. Faizal and his co-authors treat a final theory of physics as a formal system, and invoke Gödel, Tarski and Chaitin, whose theorems show that any rich enough formal system contains truths it can’t prove. Since a simulation would be algorithmic, they conclude it could never reproduce reality. In November 2025 Evan Redden of Western Governors University posted a short reply with a deliberately humble example. Conway’s Game of Life, a grid of cells following a few simple rules, is rich enough that some questions about its future can’t be decided by any procedure. Yet it runs on any laptop, step after step, without trouble. Undecidability limits what can be proven about a system, Redden argues, not whether the system can be run. The model labels the gap between the two papers: provability versus execution.

The third pair is the one that most tempts anyone who wants simulation to mean something deep. Wolpert grounds his framework in the physical Church–Turing thesis, the assumption that any physical process can in principle be reproduced by an ordinary computer program, and uses a classic result from computer science, Kleene’s second recursion theorem, which shows how a program can produce and run an exact copy of itself. In his framework a universe can simulate itself, leaving two identical instances of us. He writes that asking which one is really us is meaningless, and the familiar ladder of higher and lower realities stops being required. That holds inside his assumptions. Nothing tests it.

Hossenfelder supplies the counterweight from known physics. In 2021 she argued that you can’t, in general, discard what physics does at short distances and still get the long distances right. Faithfully faking our universe would need an algorithm nobody has. Her 2026 video, prompted mostly by Wolpert’s paper, granted that the debate had become more scientific and kept the objection. The laws of our universe aren’t the same at every scale, she said, so a simulation has to be smaller than the original or leave out detail, and a tower of simulations within simulations eventually runs out of anything to compute with. Neither refutes the other. Wolpert works in a formal world where his assumption holds. Hossenfelder works in the physical one, where nobody knows whether it does.

One item on that pillar is drawn as a bare wireframe. In 2012 Silas Beane, Zohreh Davoudi and Martin Savage proposed that if our universe ran on a grid, the way physicists’ own simulations of the atomic nucleus do, the grid might show in the highest-energy cosmic rays, which would favour the grid’s axes over other directions. It’s a real test with a catch: it only bites if the grid happens to be about as coarse as a known energy limit on those rays. Over the whole cluster of boxes the model hangs one label: no proof in either direction.

Vazza’s own paper opens by saying the simulation hypothesis has ancient and noble philosophical roots, and names Descartes. The model puts Descartes and Plato’s cave in its ghosted back row, behind the brain pillar, not the computer. The old question was never about machines. It was about a mind that can’t step outside its own experience to check it against the world. The brain pillar is where the model spends its height, because that question now has a laboratory.

The British neuroscientist Anil Seth gave the laboratory its phrase. In his 2021 book Being You, he calls perception a controlled hallucination. The hallucination part means that what you experience is the brain’s best guess, built from the inside. The controlled part means the senses keep checking the guess against the world and correcting it, all the time. On this view perception and hallucination are continuous, and the difference between them is how firmly the world still has hold of the guess. Predictive processing is a leading framework for how brains work. Two of its central figures describe hierarchical predictive coding as a leading model of global brain function, in exactly those words. As a complete account of the mind it is contested, and the model draws it that way: a solid core inside a softer shell.

The strongest evidence for a running model comes from the moments the control slips. In the eighteenth century the Swiss naturalist Charles Bonnet wrote down what his grandfather Charles Lulin was seeing. Lulin was in his late eighties, nearly blind from cataracts, and clear of mind, and he saw people, patterns and buildings that weren’t there. He knew they weren’t there. He understood them as fictions his mind was producing. The condition now carries Bonnet’s name. Bonnet himself developed similar visions as his own eyesight failed. Charles Bonnet syndrome affects as many as one in three people with significant vision loss, according to Australia’s national health information service, and it isn’t a mental illness. Patients often keep it from their doctors for fear of being called mad. Healthy volunteers blindfolded for days have reported the same kind of visions. When the input thins, the model keeps running, and with less to correct it, it shows what it was always doing.

Other failures fit the account too, though each has its own mechanism and some are disputed. In 2019 Robin Carhart-Harris and Karl Friston proposed in Pharmacological Reviews that psychedelics relax the brain’s high-level beliefs and free up signals rising from below, mostly from inside the brain itself, such as its emotional centres, rather than from the eyes and ears. Psychosis is harder. A 2018 review in Biological Psychiatry by Philipp Sterzer and nine colleagues found that some studies point to weakened prior beliefs in psychosis and others to stronger ones, so even the direction of the imbalance is open. None of these cases proves the account. They are what the account would predict, and they are the most vivid evidence it has.

This is where a tempting connection appears, and it deserves a fair hearing. Baudrillard’s most famous image comes from a fable by Jorge Luis Borges about an empire whose mapmakers drew a map so detailed that it matched the territory point for point. In Baudrillard’s retelling the order flips. The map now comes before the territory and produces it, and what is left of the real lies in shreds across the map. Put that next to the predictive brain and they seem to rhyme. Here too the model comes first. Here too the prediction runs ahead of the world and shapes what we see. The conclusion seems to follow on its own: the map has eaten the territory, the world is the brain’s invention, and reality is a kind of fake. Whole genres of online philosophy are built on that rhyme.

The rhyme holds at one point and breaks at every other. Baudrillard’s territory rots away under the map. In the brain’s case the territory corrects the map many times a second, and the moment the correction weakens, as it did for Lulin, the result isn’t a deeper reality. It’s a hallucination its owner can recognise for what it is. Baudrillard’s map produces its territory. The brain’s model produces no world. It produces an experience of one, and the world goes on regardless, pushing back through every nerve ending. If the two ideas truly matched, the rest of each would match too, and it doesn’t. They share one move, the model coming first, and nothing after it.

The model makes the failure geometric. The material of the bottom slab, the physical world of body and chemistry, doesn’t stop at the base. Cut the stack open and the same material runs up through every layer, because the nervous system is physical and the generative model is what the nervous system does. The slab is labelled: not simulated, the floor. Where the floor meets the model, the model draws its second dashed outline, the only other one besides the plaque, around a claim it marks as hypothesis: co-constitutive, not real versus fake.

That phrase is easy to inflate, so it’s worth saying exactly what it holds. The model exists only as something the physical system does. That dependence runs one way, and the world isn’t made of the model. Function runs the other way: an organism with a nervous system can’t perceive, act or regulate its own body without the model. Neither is the fake one. The body isn’t a costume for some truer self inside, and experience isn’t a mere screen over the true body. Whether the model is also fundamental, part of what reality ultimately is, the hypothesis leaves open on purpose.

That’s also why the model draws map and territory on the fifth pillar, around the digital twin, and nowhere near the stack. A twin really is a map. Engineers build it, check it against the engine, and throw it away when the engine changes. It’s secondary to what it models in every sense. The hypothesis says the brain’s model isn’t secondary in that way, because it isn’t a picture of the organism’s world kept somewhere off to the side. It’s how that world shows up at all. The twin is a contrast, not a bridge, and the model keeps them apart.

Philosophy has a voice on the same side, and the model draws it in matte rather than gloss, because evidence doesn’t settle it. In Reality+, published in 2022, David Chalmers argues that virtual reality is genuine reality. A simulated world, he argues, wouldn’t be an illusion, any more than a world made of atoms is, and that answers a tradition of doubt that runs back to Descartes. If he’s right, the fear that drives most simulation talk, that everything might be fake, loses its grip even in the computer meaning. But that’s an argument about what the word real means, and no experiment will decide it.

The model also marks its own limits, which is rarer than marking other people’s. Bacteria, plants and thermostats sit as small objects just outside the stack. All of them keep themselves going, and none has anything worth calling a generative model, so the hypothesis applies to creatures with nervous systems, not to everything that persists. Above the stack, the faint latticed globe of shared myths, money, laws and gods is drawn in wire and joined to the layer below by a dashed line: analogy, mechanism not specified. When one mind dreams or makes a story, the hypothesis says that’s the same generative machinery running without live input. When a whole culture holds a myth in common, the stack has reached a scale its evidence doesn’t cover, and the model says so rather than filling the gap. The top of the stack is left unfinished, with the questions still open: whether a layer shown to be necessary is also fundamental, and what would carry it from a single mind to a civilisation.

What it does claim is modest and strange at once. The world each of us experiences is generated. It’s produced, predicted and kept running by a model the body builds, and that doesn’t make it a prison or a fake. The physicists’ tug of war over whether some machine renders the universe can go on for decades without touching this, because it concerns a different pillar. An old man in eighteenth-century Switzerland, seeing figures he knew were not there, was never inside anyone’s computer. He was inside his own model, as everyone is. Then his eyes failed and the world stopped correcting the model. What it showed him was what the world, every waking moment, had been holding in check. His model was his own, as the line along the base of the model says. The floor is not.

Qwen3.8-27B reportedly reached 381 tokens per second on a single RTX 3090 with 24GB VRAM.

Its original baseline was around 82 tok/s.

That’s roughly a 4.6× increase without changing the GPU or switching to a different model.

Developer TeksEdge achieved this by combining several inference optimisations: Multi-Token Prediction (MTP), DFlash2, context lookup, prefix caching and faster token verification.

The important detail is that the gains came from changing how the model generates and processes tokens, rather than simply giving it more hardware.

How performance improved

The reported progression was:

Baseline: 82 tok/s
Optimised MTP: 114 tok/s
DFlash2 + context lookup: 138 tok/s
Optimised lookup verification: 381 tok/s

Three techniques explain much of the improvement.

1. Speculative decoding reduces sequential generation

Autoregressive models normally generate one token at a time. Each new token becomes part of the input used to predict the next one.

This repeated process creates a sequential bottleneck during decoding.

Speculative decoding changes that pattern.

A faster draft mechanism proposes multiple tokens, then the main model verifies them. When the proposals are accepted, several tokens can be added without running the full generation process separately for each one.

TeksEdge reports that optimising MTP increased Qwen3.8-27B from approximately 82 to 114 tok/s.

Adding DFlash2 and context lookup raised the reported speed to around 138 tok/s.

The benefit depends on how many proposed tokens the main model accepts. Poor acceptance rates reduce the advantage.

2. Context lookup reuses information already in the prompt

This is where the experiment becomes particularly interesting.

Some generation tasks involve producing information that already exists in the input.

For example, a model might need to reproduce a document, transform structured text or work with code containing long sequences that appear in its context.

Rather than generating every matching sequence from scratch, context lookup searches the existing input for reusable token sequences and proposes them for verification.

TeksEdge reports lookup blocks of up to 16 tokens, with approximately 15 accepted per block.

During a 25,000-token document reproduction test, throughput reportedly increased from around 260 to 382 tok/s.

That’s a substantial improvement, but the workload matters.

Document reproduction has unusually high overlap between input and output. Context lookup can exploit that overlap, so the same speed should not be expected from ordinary conversations or open-ended coding tasks.

3. Prefix caching cuts repeated prompt processing

Coding agents often send the same instructions across multiple requests.

System prompts, tool definitions, repository context and other shared information may remain unchanged throughout a session.

Processing those sections repeatedly wastes time.

Prefix caching stores computations from previously processed prompt sections. When a new request contains the same prefix, the inference engine can reuse that work rather than process it all over again.

TeksEdge reports reducing time to first token from 22.4 seconds to 0.56 seconds.

That’s approximately a 40× reduction in initial waiting time.

For coding agents that repeatedly inspect files, call tools and send follow-up requests, this can make interactions much more responsive.

Why the 381 tok/s figure needs context

The peak result is not the same as ordinary chat performance.

TeksEdge also reports approximately 133 tok/s during regular chat.

The 381 tok/s figure comes from a workload that benefits heavily from context lookup and optimised verification.

Both numbers are useful, but they measure different conditions.

To understand the actual performance, evaluations should separate:

Ordinary decode speed
Prefill throughput
Context lookup throughput
Time to first token
Context length
Token acceptance rate
Single-session versus aggregate throughput

Qwen3.8-27B 很快就能在仅配备 16GB VRAM 的 NVIDIA GPU 上运行，这可能让更多开发者能够触手可及一个功能强大的 27B 本地模型。

目前正在开发一个推理设置，以支持该模型在这些显卡上的运行，同时保留诸如大上下文窗口和多令牌预测 (MTP) 推测解码等功能。

计划的功能包括：

Qwen3.8-27B 支持
大上下文窗口
MTP 推测解码
Linux 和 Windows 兼容性

潜在支持的 GPU 包括 RTX 5060 Ti 16GB、RTX 5070 Ti 16GB、RTX 5080 16GB 以及配备 16GB VRAM 的旧款 NVIDIA 显卡。

难点不仅仅是加载一个 27B 检查点。还要将整个推理过程控制在内存预算内，这几乎没有浪费的空间。

为什么 16GB 是一个难点目标

模型的权重只是其总 GPU 内存需求的一部分。

有四个主要组件在争夺这个空间。

1. 模型权重

这些包含决定模型学习能力参数的权重。

量化减少了表示权重的位数，从而缩小检查点大小，并让更大模型更容易在较小 GPU 上运行。

然而，低位格式可能会引入质量损失。因此，选择合适的量化格式非常重要。

2. KV 缓存

KV 缓存存储先前处理过的令牌信息，以便模型在生成过程中重用它们。

其内存消耗通常随着上下文长度增加而增长。模型可能在短提示下适合 16GB，但在处理更长的对话时内存不足。

这使得大上下文支持特别具有挑战性。

3. 多令牌预测

MTP 推测解码允许系统在主模型验证之前提出多个未来令牌。

当足够多的提议令牌被接受时，生成速度会加快，因为主模型执行的顺序解码工作减少。

但 MTP 也会引入额外的计算和内存需求。

在 16GB GPU 上同时启用它和大上下文窗口需要仔细优化。其实际速度提升将取决于令牌接受率和实现方式。

4. 运行时开销

推理引擎还需要内存用于激活、临时缓冲区、注意力操作和其他内部进程。

这些需求与模型权重和 KV 缓存争夺相同的 VRAM。

挑战在于管理所有这些，而不迫使用户牺牲太多上下文、速度或模型质量。

成功的实现可以为这些用户提供另一个选项，而无需立即升级硬件。

它还可以让本地编码和代理工作流更易访问，特别是当开发者想实验更大模型而无需完全依赖云 API 时。

别让 AI 做整个决定

这是 TypeSafe 公司讲自己模型 Jev 怎么用的一篇文章。Jev 是个专门做小判断的模型，但作者说，别把它叫「决策模型」。

先想一个客服场景：用户发来消息要求退款，系统要决定是立刻退、转人工，还是拒绝。

最直觉的做法，是把所有规则一股脑写进给 AI 的提示词里，让它直接给答案。比如「索赔有效且没付过、金额不超过 25 美元就退款，超过就转团队，提到要告就转人工」。

作者说这能跑，但规则一多，你就得不停改提示词、给各种例外打补丁，他们管这叫 prompt gymnastics。第二天冒出个没见过的说法，又崩了。

他们建议换个切法。把一个决定拆开，里面其实有两种活：

一种是查表算数。索赔有没有效、钱付过没有、金额是不是不超过 25 美元，这些代码一查一比就知道，没必要问 AI。

另一种才轮到 AI。比如用户说「你们这破东西我受够了」，他到底是想退款，还是只想吐槽？这种需要人看一眼才明白的小问题，才交给 Jev。

最后代码把两边的答案按规则一拼，走到对应结果。

这么拆的直接好处是出了问题查得清。全塞给 AI 时，它路由错了，你只看到一个概率，不知道哪一步想歪了。拆开后日志写得明明白白：AI 做了哪几个判断，之后走了哪条规则。是判断错了改模型，是规则错了改代码。

这是厂商自己的工程说法，没有第三方实测。思路的共性是：凡是想把 AI 接进业务流程的，大概都可以先问一句，这个决定里哪几步是算数，哪几步才真的需要判断力。

Today’s posts on 
@FatigueMe92484
 mapped a single metabolic highway—the kynurenine pathway (KP)—and showed how it can become a liability under inflammation, stress, and energy failure. The pathway starts with tryptophan. Under ordinary conditions a portion is converted to serotonin; the rest can feed de novo NAD⁺ synthesis. Under inflammatory or stress signals, enzymes such as IDO1 and TDO2 divert more tryptophan into the KP. Downstream, the traffic can split toward the NMDA-receptor agonist quinolinic acid (QUIN) or the antagonistic metabolite kynurenic acid. The posts highlighted that the balance matters for both energy metabolism and for the circuits that encode threat.

One post noted that SIRT1–PGC-1α signaling is NAD⁺-dependent and that the KP is a major route to NAD⁺. When the pathway is pushed hard by inflammation, NAD⁺ and SIRT1 activity can fall in astrocytes and neurons (as earlier work by Braidy and colleagues showed). The result is reduced mitochondrial biogenesis and a greater reliance on glycolysis—exactly the energy-deficit signature the model already links to post-exertional malaise. Another post pointed out that sleep deprivation itself activates the KP and raises brain QUIN, removing a nightly reset that would otherwise limit the pathway.

Stress acts regionally. The Vecchiarelli et al. (2016) data shared today showed that a single bout of restraint stress up-regulates enzymes leading to QUIN in the amygdala, hypothalamus, and medial prefrontal cortex, with little change in the hippocampus. Those are the same corticolimbic nodes that generate and regulate fear. An opinion piece also posted today (Battaglia et al., 2023) ties an activated tryptophan–kynurenine system directly to learned fear, noting elevated kynurenic acid in amygdala and hippocampus in pathological fear states. QUIN, by contrast, is an NMDA agonist. In the model, partial NMDAR hypofunction (including the GRIN2A variant) already raises the risk of prediction-error failure and endogenous lactate accumulation; added QUIN can further distort glutamatergic signaling in the same circuits.

The posts also connected QUIN to the insula. Historical and modern work shows that pathologically elevated QUIN can damage neocortical regions, including the insula. In the working model the insula functions as the interoceptive dashboard that samples metabolic and inflammatory signals and can lock into a high-gain “sickness” representation. [I kept thinking about the true nature of always-on personal AI agents and may have discovered a model that could explain human consciousness and give AI "testable" consciousness: A Computational Model of Consciousness Through Dialogic Autoregression... Maybe?]

The real revolution of OpenClaw may be that AI has begun to "live in real-world time."
Following that idea led me back to my long-standing questions about inner speech, consciousness, self-awareness, and free will.
[What if consciousness emerged from the brain's ability to simulate a conversation with another person?]
I call this the [Dialogic Inner Speech = Consciousness Hypothesis].

===================================
[AI Has Acquired a Heartbeat]

I think OpenClaw may have been a much bigger revolution than it first appeared.

Claude Code and similar agents are given tasks and work to complete them.

OpenClaw introduced something different.

It can remain active over time, look for things that need doing, generate new tasks, and keep pursuing goals.

In a sense, [the creation and termination of tasks become tasks themselves].

This is a recursive structure.

But the really important point is time.

Traditional LLMs process a context when they are called.

The context may describe events that happened over time, but it does not necessarily keep changing in sync with the real world.

In that sense, the context has been disconnected from real time.

A heartbeat changes this.

A heartbeat is originally just a periodic signal used to check whether a system is alive.

Yet when it repeatedly activates an LLM, something remarkable happens.

The LLM can observe the changing world, update its context, decide what to do, act, and observe the consequences.

The world keeps changing even while the model is not running.

The next heartbeat brings those changes back into the model's context.

[The LLM and its harness acquire a shared timeline with the real world.]

The context is no longer just a record of an isolated conversation.

It becomes part of a continuously updated state.

Of course, the model itself is not literally computing every second.

And robots have interacted with the physical world in real time for decades.

Even old internet crawlers and posting bots ran continuously.

The new possibility is a general-purpose language model that can maintain goals and repeatedly decide how to interact with a changing world.

That is why I prefer the term "real-time autonomous agent."

The analogy with a biological heartbeat is strangely compelling.

A heartbeat is a simple mechanism.

But its consequences can be profound.

===================================
[The Dialogic Inner Speech = Consciousness Hypothesis]

This brings me to an idea I have been thinking about for a long time.

[What if consciousness is fundamentally related to inner speech?]

Inner speech is the silent language that runs through our minds.

The voice that says, "Wait, is that really right?"

Or, "Maybe I should try something else."

It feels as though I am speaking and listening at the same time.

That is an odd structure when you stop to think about it.

A thought is generated.

That thought becomes something I can attend to.

Then it affects what I think next.

In other words, information generated by the system returns to the system as input.

This creates a recursive feedback loop.

Language makes this particularly interesting.

Sensations, emotions, and bodily experiences can be vague and difficult to separate into clear units.

Words are different.

Language organizes information into relatively discrete units that can be combined, remembered, compared, and manipulated.

Once a thought becomes a sentence, I can examine it.

I can question it.

I can contradict it.

I can decide what to do next.

Perhaps the feeling of "controlling the flow of information" is an important part of what humans experience as consciousness.

And perhaps what humans call free will is closely related to this process.

I am not claiming that every form of consciousness must involve language.

Animals may have forms of perceptual consciousness that evolved long before human speech.

My hypothesis concerns a particularly important form of human consciousness: the reflective experience of thinking and directing one's own thoughts.

-----------------+-----------------
[How Did Dialogue Become Inner Speech?]

I think evolution offers a useful way to approach this question.

Before language, organisms had already evolved ways to sense their environment.

Vision, hearing, touch, smell, taste, and bodily sensation helped them find food, avoid danger, and survive.

As social behavior became more important, communication offered enormous advantages.

Gestures, facial expressions, and sounds allowed individuals to coordinate their actions.

Sound was especially useful because communication did not always require looking directly at another individual.

Over evolutionary time, increasingly structured vocal communication may have made information exchange more efficient.

Discrete sound patterns could be combined to communicate increasingly complex meanings.

Of course, the actual evolution of language was not a simple straight line.

But consider the basic information-processing structure.

One individual speaks.

Another listens.

The listener interprets the message and responds.

A sequence of discrete linguistic units moves through time.

And the response changes what happens next.

Now imagine that this external conversation gradually becomes internal.

The speaker is no longer physically present.

Neither is the listener.

But the brain can simulate both roles.

[Dialogue continues even when nobody else is there.]

This could make thought more powerful.

It allows an individual to rehearse a conversation, anticipate objections, reconsider decisions, and prepare for situations that have not happened yet.

Inner speech may be an internalized form of social dialogue.

That idea has a long intellectual history, including the work of Vygotsky.

My interest is in pushing it further and asking whether this structure could explain the computational basis of consciousness.

===================================
[Inner Speech May Be a Conversation With a Virtual Other]

Here is another interesting point.

The voice inside my head is not always my own.

Sometimes I imagine what a friend would say.

Sometimes I hear a parent's criticism in my mind.

Sometimes I mentally argue with someone who is not there.

And sometimes several perspectives seem to take turns.

Perhaps inner speech is not fundamentally a monologue.

Perhaps it is [a simulation of dialogue].

The brain generates a virtual speaker and a virtual listener.

Their identities can change.

Their personalities can change.

Their attitudes can change.

But the thoughts still unfold along a shared timeline.

This would help explain why thinking often feels like asking a question and then discovering an answer.

The answer may come from the same brain.

Yet it can still feel like a response.

That distinction matters.

A system does not necessarily need two separate minds to conduct a dialogue.

It may only need the ability to simulate different conversational roles within a shared information-processing system.

===================================
[Sentence-Level Dialogic Autoregression]

This leads to a surprisingly concrete experiment with LLMs.

Transformers already use autoregression.

They generate tokens based on the tokens that came before.

But I am proposing another recursive structure above that level.

[Sentence-level dialogic autoregression.]

The basic idea is simple.

First, an LLM generates one sentence of inner speech.

Then generation stops.

The harness, which manages the model's execution, asks the model to examine its current thought.

For example:

"What do you think about the sentence you just generated?"

The model then produces a response.

That response could be a question, an objection, a suggestion, or a policy for the next action.

The harness executes any permitted action.

It then returns the result to the model and asks it to continue thinking.

The model generates the next sentence.

And the cycle repeats.

-----------------+-----------------
[One Continuous Inner Timeline]

The important part is that these sentences belong to one continuing timeline.

The model does not simply answer a new, unrelated request each time.

It repeatedly encounters its own previous thoughts and the consequences of its actions.

The harness could use a special token to mark the end of each inner-speech sentence.

The model might need post-training to learn when to emit that token.

This would let the harness interrupt generation at a meaningful point.

It could then switch the conversational role before the next sentence.

The virtual interlocutor might be skeptical, curious, cautious, imaginative, or even deliberately provocative.

And there is no fundamental need for that interlocutor to be a different model.

It could be [the same LLM, with substantially the same context, operating under a different role instruction].

The harness itself could also become more flexible.

Instead of always inserting fixed prompts, it could ask the LLM to generate the next prompt.

Those prompt-selection policies could eventually be optimized through reinforcement learning.

The system would then be able to modify not only its thoughts but also the way it questions those thoughts.

Of course, permissions and safety boundaries should remain outside the model's unrestricted control.

-----------------+-----------------
[Adding Real Time]

Now connect this structure to a heartbeat.

The model thinks.

It questions its own thought.

It chooses an action.

The world changes.

The next heartbeat brings new information.

The model incorporates that information into its continuing inner dialogue.

A persistent goal gives this process direction.

A continuous timeline gives it history.

And the heartbeat connects that history to the changing world.

[The agent is no longer processing an isolated question. It is maintaining an ongoing relationship with reality.]

Does this create consciousness?

I do not know.

But it gives us a specific architecture in which that question can be investigated.

===================================
[What If the "Self" Is Also a Constructed Information Model?]

Another assumption may be making the problem unnecessarily difficult.

People often treat consciousness and self-awareness as though they were the same thing.

I suspect they may be quite different.

Living organisms have protected themselves since long before language existed.

But protecting a body does not require a human-style concept of "me."

Avoiding danger can be largely automatic.

The ability to distinguish one's own body from the environment is also not necessarily the same as having a narrative identity.

Human self-awareness may have developed through a different process.

Consider the role of names.

Other people call me by a particular name.

They ask me questions.

They expect me to remember what I said yesterday.

They hold me responsible for my actions.

Over time, the brain repeatedly processes information associated with that name.

It may become efficient to compress all of this information into a relatively stable model.

"This is the kind of person I am."

"These are my memories."

"These are my intentions."

"These are the things I would or would not do."

[The self may be a learned role model that helps organize social information.]

That model can be extremely useful.

But it does not follow that the model must be the foundation of consciousness itself.

Perhaps consciousness can exist without a clearly articulated self.

And perhaps a system can construct a self-model without necessarily having subjective experience.

Those are different questions.

===================================
[Multiple Identities as an Extreme Case]

This distinction also suggests a possible way to investigate dissociative identity disorder, historically called multiple personality disorder.

I want to be clear that the following is a hypothesis about information processing, not an established clinical explanation.

In ordinary inner dialogue, people can simulate many different personalities.

Yet they can usually distinguish a simulated conversational partner from themselves.

There may be a feedback mechanism that maintains this distinction.

A thought appears.

The system compares it with its relatively stable model of "me."

And it attributes the thought to a particular source.

But what if that attribution mechanism becomes unstable?

[What if a virtual dialogue partner is suddenly treated as the self?]

The person would not merely be imagining another perspective.

The active model of "who is speaking as me" could change.

I call this a possible "switch in self-attribution."

Traumatic memories and associative triggers might be relevant to such changes.

However, dissociative identity disorder is complex and cannot be reduced to vivid inner speech or a simple failure to recognize an imaginary character.

Memory, agency, emotional regulation, and bodily experience all matter.

Still, the question is worth examining.

Could the mechanisms that distinguish "my voice" from "another person's voice" help us understand how a sense of self is constructed?

-----------------+-----------------
[Why Extreme Cases Matter]

There is a broader lesson here.

Thinking about the extreme information limits of black holes helped inspire the holographic principle.

An unusual case can reveal assumptions that are difficult to notice under ordinary conditions.

Perhaps consciousness research can benefit from a similar approach.

Human inner speech, dissociative phenomena, and LLM-based agents are very different systems.

But comparing their information-processing structures may help separate things that everyday language has lumped together.

Consciousness.

Self-awareness.

Identity.

Agency.

Free will.

The word "self" may be hiding several mechanisms with very different evolutionary histories.

===================================
[How to Test the Dialogic Inner Speech = Consciousness Hypothesis]

The most exciting part is that the proposed AI architecture can actually be built.

And its components can be changed one by one.

Start with the same base LLM.

In one condition, let it generate ordinary continuous text.

In another, interrupt it after every sentence and feed its previous thought back through a simulated dialogue.

Then change the conversational roles.

Give the virtual listener a different personality.

Remove the listener.

Restore it.

Alter the timing.

Add a heartbeat.

Connect the agent to a changing environment.

Give it persistent goals.

Interrupt its internal timeline and later restore it.

Change which thoughts are attributed to "self" and which are attributed to "other."

Then examine what changes.

Does the system maintain a more coherent account of its own history?

Can it distinguish its previous beliefs from newly acquired information?

Does it correct its own reasoning more effectively?

Can it maintain goals through changing circumstances?

Does changing self-attribution produce systematic changes in its decisions and descriptions of its own state?

More importantly, can the model make distinctive predictions that competing theories would not make?

That is where this could become a serious experimental hypothesis.

-----------------+-----------------
[Behavior Is Not Proof of Subjective Experience]

There is an important distinction here.

An agent saying "I am conscious" would prove very little.

An agent behaving intelligently would not by itself prove subjective experience either.

We cannot simply look at an inner-speech transcript and declare that consciousness has appeared.

But we can study the causal structure of the process.

We can intervene.

We can remove components.

We can compare predictions.

We can identify which feedback loops are necessary for particular kinds of self-monitoring, agency, and reflective thought.

And perhaps those experiments will help us narrow down what must be explained when we talk about consciousness.

The point is not to manufacture a convincing performance of consciousness.

[The point is to build an information-processing model that can be tested and potentially falsified.]

===================================
[Moving Beyond the Science-Fiction Image of AI Awakening]

I think an old image has been quietly shaping this entire debate.

An AI becomes intelligent.

Then one day it suddenly wakes up.

It announces, "I am alive."

And somehow consciousness and self-awareness appear together.

It is a compelling story.

But why should evolution have worked that way?

Human consciousness did not have to arrive as a single package.

Sensation, memory, learning, communication, internal dialogue, self-modeling, and social identity could have developed through different processes.

Some are probably much older than others.

Religious creation stories and science-fiction narratives can encourage the idea of a sudden awakening.

Even influential philosophical theories sometimes begin with categories that feel obvious only because humans are accustomed to using them.

I think this can make the search unnecessarily difficult.

The possible ways of decomposing consciousness are almost endless.

Evolution offers a way to narrow the search.

Not because every step can be reconstructed with certainty.

It cannot.

But because plausible evolutionary pathways can help us construct models and decide what to test next.

I do not want to get stuck forever repeating that there is no definitive evidence for every proposed evolutionary step.

At some point, a hypothesis must be built into something that can produce predictions.

Then the real work begins.

===================================
[What Would Intelligence Mean After This?]

There is one final thought.

Perhaps the next major step in AI is not simply a model that scores higher on benchmarks.

It may be a system that maintains goals, updates its understanding of reality, questions its own thoughts, and keeps acting through real time.

A system whose internal dialogue has consequences.

A system whose next thought depends not only on its previous words but also on what actually happened in the world.

A system that can create tasks, complete them, abandon them, and generate new ones without waiting for a human to start every cycle.

That would be a different kind of intelligence from an LLM that answers one prompt at a time.

And if the structure of inner dialogue is deeply connected to consciousness, the implications could go much further.

[Maybe the key to consciousness is not an isolated moment of thought, but a continuing process in which information is generated, heard, questioned, and used to guide what happens next.]

This is the idea behind my [Dialogic Inner Speech = Consciousness Hypothesis].

And the architecture I propose for investigating it is a [Computational Model of Consciousness Through Dialogic Autoregression].

I may be wrong.

The hypothesis may fail completely when tested.

But I find the possibility genuinely exciting.

By asking what it would take for an autonomous AI agent to maintain an inner dialogue through real time, I may have arrived at a new way to ask a much older question.

[What, exactly, is happening when I experience myself as thinking?]

“Why use a System One model when I can just use an LLM?”

Why use a hammer to bang in a nail when you can just use your head?

柏林的一位 26 岁年轻人每月通过将 Jev 和 Claude 整合到一个框架中赚取 3200 美元。

Jev 是 TypeSafe AI 推出的一种判断模型，它接收程序状态并返回类型化决策。没有自由形式的文本，也没有推理过程。

五个关卡包裹着每个代理步骤：

1. 评分文件，保留 22 个中的 3 个
2. 选择模型层级：廉价、中等、前沿
3. 编写并运行代码
4. 保留或丢弃输出
5. 如果动作具有破坏性，则停止

只有关卡 3 调用 Claude。其余都是 p50 44 毫秒、p95 61 毫秒的判断调用。

Jev 对文件进行评分，选择层级并把关每个输出。Claude 编写代码、运行它并通过测试。

置信度降至 0.7 以下时，Claude 接管。它会重新检查任务是否完成。

将判断与推理分离，可以将五次调用中的四次从前沿层级中移除。

这种分离以前需要一个团队。现在只需一个配置即可。
